segments.text: The largest decrease. The projections were that between 2024 and 2026, we'd actually see somewhere between a 29% and a 46% decrease in development assistance for health. And all health issues are not created equal.

Reproductive health, you guessed it, would land around 54% of that decrease. And you'll know that certain restrictive policies, particularly the US government and others, directly tackle some of these issues, which hampers the funding that we have. So our financial needs are getting greater.

But the governments that used to rely on these resources are getting squeezed in other ways. In 2025, Africa's debt service was $81 billion, which is actually more than they received in grants, in development aid. And so we're seeing that in about a third of countries writ large, the governments are spending more on servicing debt than they are on either their health line or their education line.

So on some of the social services. So what does this mean? We saw some encouraging, if we can go to the next slide, we saw some encouraging reactions to, oh, sorry, I can give you some more details on what this means. Who's driving the cut and what does it mean in practice? 57% of this is actually driven by the United States, but 57% cut of US funding given the actual US economy generates a three quarter drop in sort of the financing globally.

That's how big it is. And so when the US cut their funding, at the same time, the five biggest donors for our issues all cut their funding. So you saw Japan, sorry, Japan, Germany, the US, UK and France all cut their funding, mostly because they were reinvesting into the security agenda, which means that they caused 96% of that fall.

Now, this has a direct impact on services. In earlier last year, WHO right on the back of the cuts undertook its pulse survey, which reaches 108 countries to see what was actually happening on the ground. And 70% of the countries said within a couple of months when this was done that they were already seeing cuts to essential services that affect women, children and adolescents.

50 countries or more actually reported losses in health workforce, right? So we're seeing effects on the health workforce. The findings weren't necessarily specifically midwifery because the data wasn't disaggregated that way, but the whole health workforce. And then we ran a parallel survey this year of our partners in 67 countries and saw that 80% are still affected by funding cuts, 69% of which have seen a close in actual programs because of that.

What does this mean for midwifery? That we have limited data on this, but UNFPA issued some information last year noting that they would only be able to support 47% of the midwives that they were meant to support. So if you're looking at a figure that's 3,521, it would be roughly half of that. And so that halves the number of midwives that you can deploy in Gaza and Yemen and everywhere else.

And we're seeing from modeling that this projects a 45% increase in mortality from maternal mortality. Now, if you go on to the next slide, the response to this can only be domestic resource mobilization. And we saw a lot of governments very actively take a stake and say, we will increase our funding because the model currently doesn't work.
It leaves us exposed and we need to do something. But we know that despite all of the goodwill, this is something that's relatively hard to do. The Abuja commitment was made in 2001.

I think we're 25 years beyond that now. Only three countries have regularly, and maybe not systematically, but regularly attained that goal. And some people will say that it is just a percentage-based target and we should be looking at actual numbers.

Well, then WHO recommends that $86 be spent per capita, per annum, in order to fund essential services for women, children, and adolescent health. And we know that roughly half of the countries on the continent can't get to that 86%. So while domestic resource mobilization is the direction we're moving in, it's something that's hard for us to do.

If we go to the next slide, so what does that mean for who pays for the services? People. Unfortunately, the burden then comes onto the women who seek healthcare. 35.6, so 36% of health services or health spending is covered by people.

And a lot of these people often face catastrophic out-of-pocket expenses. And with the trends that we're seeing now, with the shortages in development funds and governments having issues with upping their resources, we risk reversing this. So what do we do? Can we go to the next slide? There's a lot of research that's been going on here, but that's not new research.
And we already know what needs to be done. We operate within governments that have revenue. And so their revenue envelope serves as the basis for what it is that they can spend.

So there are a number of things that we can do. One is to work with the government to help increase the general resource envelope. And so part of the conversation that we need to have with ministries of health is to not go to them and say, we need more money, but sometimes to help them in that conversation about where they can get those additional resources.

Part of what we're doing at the PMNCH with the financing campaign is looking at some of the spaces that are important for countries. So what can we do in terms of advocacy for debt relief? The second thing is to strengthen financial performance management, right? So a lot of the resources that we have end up either being allocated or they're not allocated, or they are allocated, they're not disbursed. There are many steps within the management line that have us lose money.

So how do we improve resources from that level? Innovative finances and innovative use of taxes. Are we building levies? Are we building taxes on alcohol, on sugar, on tobacco, or on things that are sin taxes that are unhealthy? But one of the things that's quite interesting is we actually have the higher proportion of countries in the Africa region that do undertake those taxes, but in many cases, they're actually not then allocated to the health sector. So part of the question is also around where those resources are allocated and are they coming to the right sector? Now in terms of better use of funding, that's another thing that we can take to the government.

In 2010, WHO's report found that 20 to 40% of health resources were wasted, right? And so there are inefficiencies for us to work on and there are inefficiencies for us to work on in our realm here because Africa CDC actually says that the biggest health spending, 55% of the general health budget, is for the workforce. So we need to think through how do we work more effectively? How are we prioritizing essential interventions? How are we putting midwifery into PHC and national UHC packages and delivering on that? And then there are things that look around how we pool resources. So what can we do from a regional manufacturing, market shaping perspective? Pooling asks for commodities as well as working better together so that different donor partners are not wasting resources because of vertical programming.
Now specifically linked to, can we go to the next slide? Specifically linked to midwifery, I think that means a couple of things. And we know what to do. Partners have started talking about it.
Dan referenced it, Frida referenced it earlier today. There is, we need to make sure that the money's getting channeled. That's one of the things that I just talked about.

So raising the money, making sure that we're helping the government in terms of developing that investment case, making the arguments to them, having them allocate that money to our sector. Then it's about channeling the resources and making sure that they're going into midwifery services and midwifery models of care. So building that into the primary health care as much as we can.

And then the third one, which we're all responsible for here, is to make sure that we're not putting the women themselves at risk by protecting them from out-of-pocket costs. So in so much as we can strengthen things like community-based insurance, mechanisms to pull risk writ large, or reimbursing maternity care or making those maternity care services free, then those are things that we can start to prioritize. Okay. So I start with where I'm domiciled. Okay, I'm asking the question.

Aminata, please have your mics. How has the investment case, Sierra Leone has been so much in the social media recently, and we don't know, how has the investment case, the midwifery investment case been used in Sierra Leone? To advocate for midwifery and influence policy dialogue and decision making. Okay, thank you very much.

Good afternoon, everyone. So Sierra Leone is one of the champions of the midwifery investment case. The whole idea was conceptualized in 2024, when the midwifery accelerator initiative was being discussed.
So Sierra Leone, the leadership embraced it. And like I said, we are among the champions. So the investment case has been done.

We had a very good case, a very reasonable based on the maternal and child health indices and all the surrounding service provision platforms. So we had a very interesting investment case, but based on the discussions around the midwifery accelerator, the leadership embraced, and then that led to the development of the nursing and midwifery strategic plan, and also the development of the Sierra Leone midwifery investment case, and all of that was supported by UNFPA. So what the investment case has done, in summary, in the first place, it has elevated the midwifery profile, the profile of midwifery services.

It has increased political recognition. It has increased the realization that midwifery services are essential to achieving national targets around reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health national targets that midwifery services are critical to achieving those targets. It has also created a framework for continuous government and partner engagements on midwifery services.

This also led to stronger recognition. Like I said, the investment case was used as a reference or as a resource for the development of national strategies, the National Health Sector Strategic Plan that was integrated into those plans. The investment case was used.

It was used as a resource material, and also into the RMN-CAH strategic plan and investment case also. It was also integrated. It also gave us a strengthened voice to advocate for increased domestic funding for midwifery services because the investment case demonstrated that there will be a seven US dollar return on every single dollar that was invested in midwifery services.
So that strengthened our voice in advocating. It also led to increased political commitment. The Minister of Health committed to increasing the recruitment in the number of midwives.

Initially, he stated 3,000, but after he attended the ICM in Lisbon, Portugal, he came back, reviewed the situation, and then said he will increase to 6,000. So between three and 6,000. So it also contributed to better workforce planning because we know about the challenges in remote rural districts, but the investment case made a clear case for equitable distribution training of midwives to very underserved areas.

So basically, I would say the midwifery investment case has significantly contributed because it was taken into consideration. It was integrated into national strategic documents and policies, and also included into the benefits packages, the social health insurance scheme. Midwife services was also incorporated into all of that.
So shortly in summary, I think that's basically some of the key things that the investment case has done. Thank you very much for your attention. Thank you very much.
Yes, we see the political engagement, involvement, or high political commitment, and elevating the midwifery voice and the need for investing in midwifery. Thank you. So now, we go up north.

We need to make a case of midwifery for the Ministry of Finance. And to answer this, the question is, from Egypt's experience, how can ministries of health most effectively make the case for investing in midwifery to the Ministry of Finance? I think you've heard what Katie presented. And now, please tell us your story.

Okay, first of all, for the health system, we know, of course, the importance of midwifery and the role they play. But when talking, I was negotiating with Ministry of Finance, we need to speak their language. We need to speak figures and numbers.

That's why we thought of first highlighting the challenge we, Egypt, facing. We have a very high rate of cesarean section, which is almost 72%. We have 59% out-of-pocket, our health expenditures are out-of-pocket, which is really a burden on the national and economic system in Egypt.

This was the first step. Then, we thought of developing the midwifery investment case to translate these challenges into opportunities. And actually, the investment case came up with some really good scenarios between 2026 and 2030.

I have another history, I cannot recall it by name. But the investment case shows that about 38,000 maternal and neonatal and child deaths can be averted. Around 860,000 unplanned pregnancies can be prevented.

And the health system saving is about 9.7 billion Egyptian pounds. This, in addition to the social benefits, which is equivalent to 94.8 billion Egyptian pounds that has economic value. These numbers were the case to present to Ministry of Finance.

Also, the most important thing is at Ministry of Health, they linked the midwifery program to the broader reform system, health system in Egypt. It's not a standalone program that's about training midwifery and then there is no opportunity for professional recognition or deployment or absorbing in the hierarchy of Ministry of Health. No, they linked it to the reform of the national health system, to the reform of the PhDs at the ministry.

So it's not a standalone program. Also, the most important thing and the third point that we highlighted that it's not only about training midwives. We have to build the full picture, a full reform structure for them to be absorbed and to have the professional recognition and clearly defined and approved scope of practices, deployment, funded position and employment opportunity.

Also for us, we highlighted that creating this career of midwives, it's a good opportunity for girls and women to join this career and it's kind of women empowerment. They will have an opportunity to join this career, to have their informed decision about their lives, their decisions, their pregnancy. So it's a full comprehensive program.
It's not only about making a new career. No, it's a full structure and comprehensive structure. Your Honor.

Yes, figures and numbers. What the Minister of Finance wants to hear is what do I stand to gain? What does the government stand to gain? So we must speak, figures translates those lives saved into monetary terms. Thank you so much for that.
Now, we come to the land of a thousand hills, we see. Right. We've had the issue of protection, the third factor that needs to be considered.
After we raise, we channel, we need to protect. And I've seen the OOP. In other words, they say, oops.
All right. Not so. Yes, so now in Rwanda, community-based health insurance scheme.

This is an innovative model that financing mechanism that you've adopted. And I think the minister spoke to it in the morning during the opening ceremony. This extent to extend the midwifery services.
Could you elaborate? How does it help reduce out-of-pocket expenditure? Just in brief. I know it can be very detailed, but just in the next two minutes. Thanks.

Thank you. First of all, what I can say is that CBHI, the community-based health insurance is a prepayment pooled mechanisms that has been established by the government to help households and protect them from financial catastrophic health expenditure. And it has actually been a very good instrument also to increase health insurance coverage, whereby now in Rwanda, we have more than 90% of people who are covered by health insurance.

And it has also contributed a lot to shift the financial burden of healthcare services from households to the pooled mechanisms that is CBHI. And coming back to the midwife services, and in the CBHI benefit package, all antenatal care, deliveries, health services, and also postnatal care are all included in the benefit package of CBHI. And so mothers and all other people who access those services do not really pay the full cost of those services, but instead they pay a co-payment of 200 Rwandan francs at the health center level, and only 10% of the full cost at the hospital level.
And the rest is covered by CBHI. So that has gradually reduced the out-of-pocket expenditure, where we came from 23% of OOP to 4%. Now we are at 4% of OOP, which is something that is very incredible.

And what I can say is that also with CBHI, we have been able to increase the equity, equity in the sense that people pay their premiums, their contributions to be member of CBHI according to their financial capacity, because in Rwanda we have what we call a social registry, which is managed by the Minister of Local Governance. And that social registry actually categorized people into category based on their financial means, which is actually linked with other systems that we have in Rwanda, including salaries, properties, and all other systems. And people actually contribute based on what, on their capacity.

And with that social registry, actually we also identify the vulnerable people where governments provide support for those people. So the CBHI has been a very good tool to increase also that equity, but also the inclusiveness of all, everyone, including the vulnerable people. Thanks.
Impressive. Reducing that out-of-pocket from 23 to 4% is quite impressive. Thank you so much.

And now we are here at the foundation of the moms and the babies, the CSO perspective in midwifery financing. From your perspective as a civil society organization, how can you help ensure that midwifery is prioritized in health financing decisions? Thank you so much, Dan. I've been enjoying the conversation so far.

And if I must be honest, I'm really happy that I'm kind of closing this session because the CSOs are so important. I mean, CSOs are the essential bridge between high-level decision makers and the communities and vice versa. Let me use this very basic observation we made at For Moms and Babies Foundation.
So I was the third cohort from one of the state universities back in Cameroon. And in my midwifery class were 41 of us. And out of that 41, there were 39 females and two male.

Shout out to the male midwives in the room. And currently out of the 41 of us who study midwifery, just about seven of us are currently practicing midwifery or doing something in relation to midwifery. This got me thinking.

And I actually went back to the training board as a CSO founder who is also a midwife. And going back to those schools, I realized that almost half of the student midwives were already planning on dropping out. What is the issue? Money, right? Money, and we're discussing money here today.

And the hall is so quiet. When we are talking money, everyone is like, oh, where would it come from? But it's a very, very important and sensitive topic because CSOs play a huge role. We get the stories from the ground.
We have a deeper level of understanding of the things that go on on the field. We work with these midwives. I am a midwife myself.

I'm running an organization now, kind of exposes me a lot more to the challenges that are on the field, to the difficulties that my fellow colleagues midwives face, particularly in rural and conflict-affected regions like the ones I work in. CSOs can generally help to capture this data because they are closer to the problems, closer to the issues. They can help to capture this data, get the numbers, and be able to advocate for better outcomes for midwives.

We can also share real stories from the ground. And we can also show high return on investment when it has to do with the input that midwives put into place and also the impact that they have on moms and babies and their survival. Finally, CSOs can also hold both parties.

And when I say both parties, I'm talking about the government and even the midwives who work in these areas are accountable. Accountability is a very big deal. And also looking at the aspect of interlocutors, there are so many.

I mean, I always say maternal and child health is not a one-man show. It's an issue that has to do with all hands on deck, talking from head of states right down to, you know, even the moms in the communities and particularly the midwives, because most times we have the tendency of excluding midwives from decisions that concern midwives and it should not be so. Of course, governments and, you know, people, a lot of things are happening in the background, but then if this is not properly communicated, then chances are high that, you know, their miscommunication can go into play.

For example, the student midwives I spoke about, most of them said they were told or they heard that, you know, there's no money for midwives. So that already keeps them back from, you know, going or going full head on into the field. So I know that the government is doing a lot, Cameroonian government is doing quite a lot, UNFPA too is putting hands on deck for midwives, but then it needs to be better communicated so that more people or more midwives can know that a lot of advocacy is going on in the background for their sake.

And finally, I think decentralization also is a huge aspect when we are talking about money, because most times bureaucracy gets this money stuck, you know, and we are just nowhere to be found. But then when all of this is decentralized, when we know where the money goes to and how it's being used, it makes it a lot more easier for the money to be tracked and also accountable. Thank you so much.

Thank you very much, Data for Advocacy, Accountability. And CSO's voice needs to be heard for the sake of the midwife, for the sake of the mother, for the sake of the baby, for better financing and just so ever. Thank you so much.

So lastly, I think Karim must ask you something. What do you make of this discussion that has ensued from the experiences from the countries? That's your call. Thanks, you can tell I'm the tech savvy one in my family.

No, it's been so encouraging to hear the conversation. I think one, to hear how successful the investment cases have been and the national level advocacy has been, because it's really ultimately a question of leadership. And so for me, it points to a couple of things that are takeaways for this session.

One, the critical nature of the investment case in terms of helping us speak the language of the people that we are definitely targeting. I do think that to a certain extent, we need to walk the talk as well. Some of what I've heard from ministries of finance and other partners in countries is that the landscape is complex.

And so everyone in the current instance is sort of pushing for their own issue. And I think that that's where the role of civil society and of working in coalitions becomes really important so that we're bringing everyone along and making sure that it's anchored in a sort of PHC stance. But then I think the second point is the one that was just brought up by my sister, which is getting the money allocated is one thing, but a lot of what we're hearing from partners across not just midwifery, but the other spaces is disbursement doesn't happen.

It doesn't happen in a timely way. So really working with civil society and other actors to track that money and make sure that it's reaching the right people. But I'm so humbled to see what's going on in the different countries.
Thank you very much. So, Aminata, we start with you. Only one priority action in 30 seconds.
Each one of us must. Yes. Well, actually, our investment- In 30 seconds.
While we'll continue advocating for increased domestic funding, I think that's our one priority action. Thank you. 30 seconds also? Yes.
Okay, I have three priorities. I will say it very quickly. The evidence, local evidence-based data generating the national ownership is the most important thing in this.

The international experience and technical assistance is important, but the case is really successful when it's grounded in local data and linked to national priorities. Also, the multi-sectoral coordination is very important and it is not only Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Health. There is regulatory bodies, there is syndicate, there is education entities.
They all need to work together. And finally, we need to move from funding to financing. This is the most important thing in this for me.
Thank you. And Gary? One key action points for you in 30 seconds. I would say leadership has to be more committed to funding and to raise more domestic funding.
Okay, thank you. Thank you. And mine will be to create a protected budget specifically for hiring, training, and equipping midwives.
In other words, invest in midwives. Thank you. Thank you.
